title: A Critical Review of the Story of the Ramayana and an Account of South Indian Castes
html:
A Critical Review of
THE STORY OF
THE RAMAYANA
AND
AN ACCOUNT OF SOUTH INDIAN CASTES*

BY
MR. V. P. SUBRAMANIA MUDALIAR, G. B. V. C.

INTRODUCTORY REMARKS.

The late lamented Prof. P. Sundaram Pillai, M.A., Philosophy Professor, the Trivandram College, and the author of such rare works as 'மனேன் மணீயம்' and 'திற்கிறானை விளக்கம்' evinced much interest in historical researches. His "Milestones in the History of Tamil Literature" † is a standing monument to his work in that field.

Certain truths brought to light in his researches, he did not kive to publish. His unpublished convictions on various subjects of importance are likely to be met with in his diaries, in his letters, or are engraved in the memory of those who had the fortune to converse with him on such topics. One evening in Madras, a few years before his death, he held a conversazione at which I was present. The subject of the conversation turning upon the Ramayana, one of his friends asked him for his views on the same. The views he expressed then form the basis of the present paper on the Ramayana. I do not possess either his impressive method of conveying conviction to his readers or the necessary historical training. It would have been much better if Mr. Sundaram Pillai had lived to publish his views on the subject. I expected that some of his friends better acquainted with him than myself would publish these views. As no such friend is forthcoming, I have to publish them for fear that they might otherwise be lost to the world. It is needless to add that any criticism of these views will have to be met by archaeologists who have made a study of the subject. Myself am an amateur and lay no claim to originality. The preface and the following pages are written as if they were Mr. Sundaram Pillai's.

PREFACE.

There are certain points which I should make clear to my readers before I publish my views on the Ramayana. I may without any vanity be allowed to say that I am behind few of my countrymen in point of religious fervour. Some of my views may seem irreligious at first sight. But a careful and scientific examination of the same will show that they are not actually so. I may however diverge from the popular and time-honoured, but in my opinion, misdirected beliefs regarding 'castes.' Caste system and religion are not necessarily connected with each other. So my ideas of 'caste' may differ from those of others, without in any way affecting the common religious sentiment. My views on the Ramayana have no concern with religion. But they are intimately connected with race distribution and 'caste' in the accepted sense of the word. To facilitate the enquiry, I propose to deal with the subject under three separate heads:—

  1. i. Race distribution and 'Caste' or rather the non-existence of 'caste' at the time of the Ramayana.
  2. ii. South Indian Castes prior to the time of the Ramayana.
  3. iii. South Indian Castes after the time of the Ramayana.

SECTION I.
South Indian Castes
AT THE TIME OF
THE RAMAYANA

Of the two Ithihasas Ramayana and Bhārata, the latter is considered by some historians to have had some foundation on facts. But no historical incident has as yet been brought to light which could have supplied the ground-work for the construction of the story of the Ramayana.* 'Sita' and 'Rama' are used in the Vedas to mean 'furrow' and 'water' respectively. Linguists derive the words 'Aryar' and, '\sigmai' from the same root and say that 'Aryar' means 'എട്തെയാൻ' (those owning ploughs—agriculturists). On these data some historians look upon the Ramayana as an allegorical representation of the spread of Aryan civilization in India and the conquest of South India by the Aryans. As such, the Ramayana of Valmiki would be a poem written by an Aryan poet to proclaim the prowess of the Aryans.

The merits of the Non-Aryans and the demerits of the Aryans as admitted by the Aryan poet need not be called in question. But where Valmiki mentions some prominent Dravidian princes † and enumerates the offences for which Rama fought against them, dethroned them and replaced them by men who would do his bidding, it would be worth while to enquire into the nature of the charges against the Dravidian princes deposed by Rama and the methods he adopted to conquer them.

I. The two persons whom Valmiki accuses strongly are Ravana and Vali.

(a) The charges brought against Ravana are :—

  1. i. that he incarcerated the Devas;
  2. ii. that he disturbed the peace of the Aryan 'munivars' (ascetics); and
  3. iii. that he abducted Sita.

(b) The charges levelled against Vali are :—

  1. i. that he banished Sugriva; and
  2. ii. that he took Sugriva's wife to himself.

II. The Aryan methods of conquest.

Will be discussed later on.

I. Valmiki's Culprits.

i. Ravana.—The high culture and the manifold achievements of Ravana are extolled by Valmiki himself. Ravana was an enlightened monarch, learned in the Vedas, versed in the science and art of music, and withal formidable in the battle-field. He had subjugated many lands by the strength of his arm. His subjects enjoyed peace and prosperity under his rule. His relatives received at his hands a cordial and hospitable treatment. It is not clear what Valmiki meant by describing him as a ten-headed monster with twenty hands. Perhaps the poet intended thereby to impress upon the minds of his readers the high order of intelligence and the extreme physical strength of Ravana. Otherwise the description is altogether meaningless.* ii. Vali.—Vali was a South Indian prince of wide-spread renown. His very conquest of Ravana is enough to proclaim his valour. A devout worshipper of Civa, he could admire even in his foes such virtues as obedience to parents, love towards brothers, loyalty to one's wife, faithfulness to promise, courage in the battle-field, etc. Such virtues he admired even in Rama, the enemy of his country and his race.

So much in favour of Ravana and Vali. Let us now examine what Valmiki has to say against them.

(a) The charges against Ravana

i. The incarceration of the Devas :—

The Devas were a section of the Aryan race. The Aryans gave the Dravidians the appellation of monkeys and monsters and styled themselves Suras (\kappa \mu \hat{n}) and Devas (\kappa \text{g} \mathfrak{w} \hat{n}), "gods." The Devas were thus a part of the Aryan race. If Ravana took captive a section of his foes, it is, to say the least, no detriment to his character.

ii. Disturbing the peace of the 'munivars' :—

The 'munivars' in question were Aryan ascetics who settled themselves in the Dravidian forests and acted as spies upon the Dravidians. The Dravidians tore off their mask of religion and banished them from their lands without meting out the extreme but justifiable punishment of death. Herein the generosity of the Dravidian nature is apparent.

iii. The abduction of Sita:—

When there is enmity or when war breaks out between two nations, it is customary for the one to sieze by force or

described in the Ramayana and else-where as horrible both physically and morally, it appears that the condition of being a Rakshasa depended more upon the sins committed by an individual or by his progenitors than upon the accident of birth. If this be admitted, the physical monstrosities ascribed to the Rakshasas must be regarded as the exaggerated creations of a morbid and hostile imagination. Even the Ramayana extols the beauty and grandeur of Lanka, its architectural splendour, and the efficiency of its administration. This latter was so excellent, that no thief dared to pick up any valuable thing lost on its streets. The enemies of Rama could hardly, therefore, have been so rude and uncivilised as they are generally represented." [Ed.]

stratagem the men, women, cattle, etc., belonging to the other. Now the Aryans were making their aggressive march upon the Dravidian kingdoms. And Ravana acted within his rights in imprisoning Sita. When Sita was in Lanka, she was treated with becoming princely dignity. She was placed in Asokavana, one of Ravana's best parks, with Ravana's own niece for her companion and several other maids for her attendants. Falling in love with her, Ravana pressed his suit for her hand, but he was never rude or ungentlemanly in his behaviour towards her. He would not, like a barbarian, force her into marriage with him. This is not all. Even when countless myriads of his army had lost their lives in the battle-field, even when his brother Kumbakarna and his son Indrajit had died in the fight, he would not in his blind rage destroy the life of his enemy's wife. It was not that the thought did not strike him. He thought of it and just to frighten Rama and Lakshmana he caused a lifelike effigy of Sita to be destroyed before their eyes.

This is the treatment that the Aryan Sita received at the hands of the Dravidian Ravana. But how did the Dravidian Surpanaka fare at the hands of the Aryan Lakshmana? The spirit of chivalry shone in Lakshmana when he mutilated the nose and ears of Surpanaka. And to justify the abominable action, Valmiki gravely states that the woman tried to kidnap Sita in the presence of a man—Lakshmana. Even granting that she did try to do so, could not the victor of Indrajit* find less clumsy and more honourable methods of defeating her purpose? Did Rama at least feel sorry for the atrocity his brother had perpetrated? No. How could we expect a personage, who actually killed Thataka, feel com punction for the mere mutilation of the limbs of another woman.

The abduction of Sita might have even been an act of vengeance on the part of Ravana for the injustice perpetrated on his relative Thataka and his sister Surpanaka. If so, Ravana's action requires not even the shadow of a justification. The behaviour of Ravana towards Sita and the behaviour of Rama and Lakshmana towards Thataka and Surpanaka give one an insight into the treatment accorded to women by the Dravidians and Aryans respectively. The Dravidian and Aryan civilizations need not be compared further. And we need not wonder why the Dravidians considered the Aryans 'mlechas' or barbarians.*

The description of Ravana's city, with its streets, palaces and parks, the educational attainments of men like Ravana and Hanuman, the reception accorded by Ravana to ambassadors like Hanuman and Angathan, the royal style of life allowed to Sita during the period of her imprisonment—all these go to indicate the state of Dravidian civilization as it then was.

(b) The sins of Vali.

Vali is accused of banishing his brother Sugriva and robbing him of his wife. Vali was by right of premogeniture the ruler of Kishkindha. He was for some time away-in foreign lands, Sugriva meanwhile acting as his representative in the kingdom. When Vali returned from his travels, Sugriva refused to hand over the reins of government and Vali had to fight for his crown. Eventually, Sugriva, Hanuman and other traitors were driven into exile. But their wives were allowed to remain in the land without molestation. These might have been the bare facts. There is reason to believe that Valmiki has distorted the facts favourably to Rama and Sugriva. If Sugriva did not seek his brother's life out of ambition for the crown, he would have, on Vali's death, enthroned Angathan, Vali's son, and the rightful heir to the throne. That Sugriva did not do so indicates clearly that he acted the regicide as well as the fratricide. A justification was needed for the conduct of Sugriva and Rama towards Vali. And it is probable that to supply the justification Valmiki invented the tale of Vali's coveting his brother's wife.

II. The Aryan Methods of Conquest:

i. The last words of Vali evince the high admiration he had for Rama. Vali was, besides, a valiant soldier. Under such circumstances one might reasonably ask why Rama preferred Sugriva's to Vali's friendship. As has already been hinted, Vali was strong enough to stand on his own legs. If Rama had befriended him, Vali would have reciprocated the sentiment. But certainly he would not have helped Rama, a foreigner and a new friend, against Ravana, an old friend and a Dravidian ruler like himself. With Sugriva it was otherwise. He was a benished prince and in need of help. It was likely that he would be grateful for any help offered at that juncture. Sugriva was moreover a man who had proved traitorous to his own brother. Such a man was not likely to shrink from taking the field against a Dravidian prince—Ravana—in favour of a foreign intruder—Rama. These were probably the motives that actuated Rama in befriending Sugriva and his followers and teaching them the Aryan military tatics.

Rama did not however side with Sugriva openly and run the risk of losing Vali's good-will. In case Sugriva should lose in the fratricidal war, Rama had yet the chance of trying to persuade Vali to join him against Ravana.

ii. We have seen how Rama made use of Sugriva for conquering Kishkindha. A similar stratagem was used in the case of Lanka also. Ravana's brother, Vibheeshana, was a willing tool in the hands of Rama. The Aryan writer Valmiki has endowed this Vibheeshana with many virtues in consideration of the latter's help to the Aryans against the best interests of his country and his race. The Dravidians of a later date have been foolish enough to follow Valmiki and dub Vibheeshana with the honorific title of Azhwar (>> / <|335|> <|874|> <|413|><|874|><|714|><|874|><|714|><|914|><|893|><|954|><|954|><|674|><|587|><|90|> <|413|><|874|><|714|><|674|><|584|><|654|><|893|><|683|><|91|><|654|><|654|><|683|><|683|><|682|><|691|><|54|><|684|><|673|><|674|><|683|><|681|><|462|><|684|><|688|><|684|><|887|><|94|><|459|><|418|><|683|><|418|><|678|><|681|><|681|><|678|><|678|><|871|><|688|><|908|><|684|><|958|><|588|><|948|><|680|><|914|><|673|><|678|><|918|><|683|><|948|><|678|><|908|><|683|><|908|><|938|><|984|><|908|><|679|><|988|><|990|>

Like Sugriva, Vibheeshana was a traitor and a fratricide in one. The only difference between these two persons lies in this that the latter possessed more cunning

and less courage. The one tried to gain in open fight what his brother had obtained by right of primogeniture. The other tried to gain by low cunning and treachery the kingdom owned by his brother by right of conquest. Justly or unjustly, the one had been driven into exile by his brother: the other was kept in royal state by the bounty of his brother. Not satisfied with this, Vibheeshana aspired to become king and he sought the friendship of Rama.

Valmiki contends that the unrighteous conduct of Ravana with reference to Sita was the root cause of the apostacy of Vibheeshana. It has already been noticed that the imprisonment of Sita casts no slur on Ravana's character. Even granting that the action was improper, that would be a reason for Vibheeshana's severing his connection with Ravana, and not for his acting the traitor to his country and his race. Like Vibheeshana, Kumbakarna and Indrajit pleaded the cause of Sita; but they did not like him leave Ravana in the lurch at the critical moment. They were quite prepared to fight to the death in the interests of their country and their sovereign. Kumbakarna's patriotism could not be shaken even by Vibheeshana's tempting and perhaps genuine offer of the throne of Lanka in the event of Ravana's demise in the battle-field. Vibheeshana's conduct is inexplicable on the ground that every patriot's duty is to rescue his country from the hand of oppression. Ravana might have caused trouble to the Devas and other Aryan sections, but mention is nowhere made in Valmiki of his having oppressed his subjects. What then induced Vibheeshana to debase himself at the feet of Rama and instruct him as to the vulnerable points of the Dravidian heroes? What, if not his ambition for the crown which manifested itself on Ravana's death.

The then Social Condition of India.

At the time of the Ramayana, the Aryans, it would seem, were just colonising South India. They had not yet entered into large cities. They built huts in the forests and lived in them. Caste differentiation does not seem to have existed either in South or in North India. We learn from the Ramayana that Rama with great respect and cordiality shook hands with Guha, a chief of the Nishadas, at the shores of the Ganges. It never entered his thoughts that his person might be polluted by the touch of a non-Aryan Nishada. We find again the royal guests in the house of the Vanara prince, in the Malaya hills of the South, freely moving, dining and sleeping in the midst of the courtiers of Sugriva, and fostering a brotherly feeling towards, and intimate union with, the latter prince. In their return journey to Ayodhya, we find Sita in the friendly company of Vanara ladies of high rank. We also find the royal members of Ayodhya accompanied by the brave Dravidian warriors to whose valour the victory was mainly due, entering the hermitage of the renowned Brahman Bharadvaja where a rich feast is provided for them. The Rakshasas, Vanaras, Brahmans and the royal household of Ayodhya sit together at table and partake freely of the good things placed before them. Nowhere do we find the slightest trace of that hated caste distinction—the curse of later-day India. The picture here given is that of the Social condition of the people of India three thousand years ago. If, then, the Aryan poet called other races ‘Monkeys,’ and ‘Monsters’ it indicates nothing else than the existence in him of a feeling of race hatred and contempt for neighbours.

Assuming the historicity of the Ramayana, the geographical distribution of South India would be about the following. The country between the Vindhyas and the Nizam's dominions was known the eastern portion as Dandakaranya and the western as Janasthana. It was ruled by Sūrpanakhâ acting as the representative of Ravana. To the south of Janasthana and Dandakaranya, round Mysore, ruled the Dravidian kings Neelan, Vali, etc. The Tamilagam, “the home of the Tamils,” which lay to the south of Mysore, must have been a fertile country then. Special mention is made in Valmiki of Pandia's wealth.
